The motion makes blame depend on outcomes, which are never up to anyone. Blame belongs only to what was up to the builders: how carefully they judged. The Stoics compared the wise person to an archer. The archer is responsible for drawing and aiming well; once the arrow leaves the bow, the wind is not hers. A builder who tested, audited and deployed with care has aimed well, and the gust that followed is not her fault.

Epictetus is clear that outcomes are not up to us; only our judgements and choices are. Two equally careful teams can deploy equally well-tested systems and one can cause a disaster through no difference in their conduct. Blaming that team more is blaming them for fortune. A doctor who follows the best evidence and loses a patient to a reaction nobody could have predicted is not a worse doctor than her lucky colleague.

A Virtue Ethicist will object that a good person carries the weight of harm they caused even when blameless, and a builder who calmly says it was only fortune reveals a defect of character. Carrying the weight and being to blame are different. The Stoic builder can grieve, repair and resolve to do better without accepting blame for what was never up to her. Calm is not indifference; it is clarity about what she controlled. Proportion to the harm would blame people for what happened to them rather than for what they did.

A Stoic must deny that blame scales with harm. Careful builders who assented only to what the evidence supported acted well, whatever followed. Epictetus is clear that outcomes are not up to us; only our judgements and choices are. Two equally careful teams can deploy equally well-tested systems and one can cause a disaster through no difference in their conduct. Blaming that team more is blaming them for fortune.

Blame is a judgement about a faculty that went wrong. If the builders' judgement did not go wrong, there is nothing to blame, however terrible the result. To scale blame by harm is to blame the world for being the way it is and pin it on a person. Two teams ship the same carefully audited model. One is deployed in a quiet market and one in a hospital where a rare error kills a patient. Their conduct was identical.

Blame attaches to judgement, not to fortune, so a builder who judged well and was unlucky is blameless whatever the damage. Blame is a judgement about a faculty that went wrong. If the builders' judgement did not go wrong, there is nothing to blame, however terrible the result. To scale blame by harm is to blame the world for being the way it is and pin it on a person.

The Stoics compared the wise person to an archer. The archer is responsible for drawing and aiming well; once the arrow leaves the bow, the wind is not hers. A builder who tested, audited and deployed with care has aimed well, and the gust that followed is not her fault. A ship's captain who navigated well and still lost cargo to a storm is not blamed for the storm, though he may grieve the loss.

A Utilitarian will object that blame is a tool for changing future behaviour, and its value depends on what it achieves, not on whether the builder's judgement was correct. Using blame as a tool on people who judged well teaches them nothing, because there was nothing in their judgement to correct. Blame aimed at fortune is not a tool for improvement but a way of feeling that someone paid. Bad luck can multiply the damage without adding anything to the fault, which was settled when the builders made their choices.

The harm a system does depends on fortune; the builder's judgement does not, and only judgement can deserve blame. None of this makes the harm unimportant. The builders should help repair it and learn from it, because that is what a rational and social being does. But helping repair is not the same as being to blame, and running the two together corrupts both.
